extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in comedy/entertainment (SNL viewers, fans of Tina Fey, cultural-commentary readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative reflections on comedic material — how jokes land over time, the role of satire, and how performers should reckon with past work. Focus is on TV sketch comedy (Saturday Night Live) but the principles speak to comedy broadly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment with the cultural moment
rubrics_metrics.description: Some jokes can 'land on the wrong side of the cultural moment' — not necessarily flagrantly offensive, but misaligned in ways that become more apparent with time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate jokes for temporal and cultural fit: a line that felt sharp at the time may later feel 'off' as context shifts. The article emphasizes timing and context over outright condemnation; misalignment may be subtle and only visible in hindsight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience recognition / truth requirement for comedic effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: A joke only works if people already recognize the truth inside it; 'If the audience does not see it, the joke falls flat.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire is most effective when it reflects truths the audience already recognizes rather than trying to create them. When assessing or writing satire, confirm the audience shares the referent or perception being mocked; otherwise the joke will fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounding sketches in real moments ('fair hits')
rubrics_metrics.description: Defensible satire is based on observable reality — Fey called the Palin sketches 'fair hits' because they were 'based on real moments on the campaign trail.' She said 'if it's not true, it will not be funny.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use real incidents or widely recognized behaviors as the basis for parody to support defensibility and comedic clarity. If a sketch invents false attributes about a target, it risks falling flat or being criticized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of satire — it does not (and cannot) steer public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: The show (SNL) 'does not try to control political narratives, and more importantly, it cannot.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging comedy's societal role, don't assume writers are shaping beliefs; satire more often mirrors existing public perceptions. Critiques should account for satire's reflective, not formative, function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production pace constrains immediate reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: Live/weekly comedy reacts in real time to events, leaving 'very little room for reflection in the moment' — you 'write, perform, and move on.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments of sketches made under tight deadlines should consider the production context and limited opportunity for deliberation. Later reassessment is often necessary because distance yields perspective not available at performance time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone of acknowledgment when addressing past work
rubrics_metrics.description: Understated, non-defensive admissions (e.g., 'pretty dumb' and quiet acknowledgment that some material 'landed on the wrong side') can be more resonant than dramatic confessions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creators revisit past problematic material, tone matters: measured, personal reflection without theatrical self-flagellation often carries more weight and authenticity than overt apologies or defensiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: How comedy ages — need for historical/contextual reassessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy 'ages' and creators 'adjust their perspective over time'; staying relevant involves willingness to 'look back, acknowledge where things have shifted, and continue forward.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate older material in its historical context and be open to reinterpreting or distancing from past choices. Sustained relevance depends less on never erring and more on ongoing reassessment and adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity versus vagueness in public reckonings
rubrics_metrics.description: Fey 'offered no specific jokes she now questions' and that vagueness 'makes [the reflections] more resonant,' since many people do not conduct forensic audits of their younger selves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When public figures address past work, choosing general reflection over itemized apologies can make statements feel more relatable; however, lack of specificity may also leave questions unanswered for critics seeking detail.
